What Is Account Planning?

Explainerlowob research

By lowob · 29 August 2026 · 5-minute read · Revenue

Account planning is the practice of writing, and then keeping current, a plan for growing a specific existing customer. A good plan starts from the customer's goals rather than your product list, names the people on both sides, sets objectives with measures, and assigns actions to owners. Its value comes from being used in decisions every month, not from being completed once a year.

What account planning means

Account planning applies to customers you already have, usually the 10 to 50 that matter most to revenue. For each one, the team writes down what the customer is trying to achieve, how their organisation makes decisions, where the relationship is strong or thin, and which opportunities are worth pursuing.

It is related to account-based marketing but not the same thing. Account-based marketing coordinates marketing and sales effort against a list of target accounts, often before they are customers. Account planning is the operating plan for growing one relationship, owned by the account lead and reviewed with the people who serve that customer.

CRM vendors now treat the plan as a record type. Salesforce's Account Plans feature, for example, holds an account vision, a SWOT analysis, a customer landscape of priorities and success metrics, and a competitive landscape, and Salesforce describes the plan as "a living document".

An account plan isAn account plan is not
Built around the customer's stated goalsA list of products you want to sell them
A map of named people and their influenceAn org chart copied from LinkedIn
Objectives with owners, measures and datesA forecast with a narrative attached
Reviewed and changed monthly or quarterlyA template filled in once for an annual review

Why it matters for a commercial team

Most key account programmes underperform

Gartner's 2021 survey of 69 chief sales officers found near-universal ambition for key accounts and widespread shortfall. 95% expected key accounts to grow faster than other accounts, 58% of sales organisations missed quota on them, and 46% had rebuilt the programme at least twice in seven years. Repeated rebuilds suggest the problem is the method rather than the people.

Selection is the first mistake

The same research found that customers promoted to key account status mainly because they already spend a lot were 51% less likely to increase spend. Gartner's recommendation is to set enterprise-wide criteria for growth potential, such as access to senior executives, understanding of the customer's long-term goals and willingness to partner, and to re-tier accounts as performance changes.

Internal coordination is the second

Gartner reports that 66% of key account managers say internal coordination limits their ability to plan for growth, and that managers reporting high cross-functional collaboration see on average three times the spend from key customers. A plan written by the account lead alone tends to promise things that delivery, product or finance have not agreed to.

Current plans outperform stale ones

The strongest Gartner finding concerns use, not format. Organisations that update account plans frequently and use them to guide customer decisions are three times more likely to build customer decision confidence. Gartner separately associates high decision confidence with customers being ten times more likely to make a high-quality, low-regret purchase. These are analyst figures without a published sample on the summary page, so treat them as direction rather than benchmark.

How to write a first plan

A mid-size firm can draft a usable plan for one account in two working sessions.

  1. Pick the account on potential, not size. Score your top 20 customers on growth potential and relationship access. Plan for the top three or four first.
  2. Write the customer's goals in their words. Use what they have said in reviews, board materials or public filings. If nobody on your side can state the customer's top three priorities, that is your first finding.
  3. Map the people. List the decision-makers, influencers and users, your relationship owner for each, and how strong that relationship is.
  4. Set two to four objectives. Each needs a measure, an owner and a date. "Expand into the second business unit by Q3, owner: account lead" is an objective. "Grow the account" is not.
  5. Agree it across functions. Review the plan with delivery, product and finance before it goes to the customer, so promises are deliverable.
  6. Review it on a fixed cadence. Each review updates status and records what changed and why.

In lowob's terms, each objective is a decision in the record: what was decided, the reason, the owner, the status and the expected outcome. When the outcome arrives, it is written back against the objective, so next year's plan starts from evidence rather than memory.

lowob takeaways

  • Plan around the customer's goals. A product list is a sales target, not an account plan.
  • Select on potential. Gartner's research suggests high current spend is a poor predictor of growth.
  • Write it across functions. Coordination, not effort, is where most plans break.
  • Keep it current. A plan used monthly in decisions is worth more than a thorough one filed annually.

Common questions

What is account planning in sales?

It is the practice of writing and maintaining a plan for growing one existing customer, covering their goals, key people, opportunities, objectives and the actions each owner will take.

What is the difference between account planning and account-based marketing?

Account-based marketing coordinates marketing and sales effort against a set of target accounts. Account planning is the operating plan for one relationship, usually an existing customer.

What should a key account plan include?

The customer's goals, a map of people and relationship strength, a SWOT or similar assessment, competitive position, and two to four objectives with measures, owners and dates.

How often should account plans be updated?

Monthly for the most important accounts and at least quarterly for the rest. Gartner associates frequently updated plans with stronger customer outcomes.

Next move

Ask the owner of your largest account to write the customer's top three priorities in the customer's own words. If they cannot, book a meeting with the customer to ask, and start the plan from the answer.
